units.title: Form 4 VA Intro: Course and SBA Portfolio
units.intro: Form 4 starter unit. Learn the two learning strands (appreciation and making), positive values, and the basic SBA portfolio structure (research workbook + artwork/critical studies). lessons.title: Two Strands: Appreciation and Making
cards: Form 4 Visual Arts follows the official curriculum with two main strands: visual arts appreciation and visual arts making.
Appreciation: learn to look at artworks, understand signs and styles, and the historical, social and cultural contexts of art.
Making: learn to use materials and techniques to express ideas, turning experience and feeling into visual form.
Throughout both strands, build an open and respectful attitude toward different cultures and viewpoints.
[No cleared image yet] Later: a simple two-strand diagram (self-made / CC0).

lessons.title: SBA Portfolio: Research Workbook and Artwork/Critical Studies
cards: School-based Assessment (SBA) usually means one portfolio: a research workbook plus artwork/critical studies.
Artwork/critical studies: about four pieces under one theme; some may be written critical studies (follow school and official guidance).
The research workbook shows theme exploration, study of related artworks, media experiments and reflection on progress.
Assessment focuses on media skills, visual presentation, relationship with context, creativity/imagination, overall theme communication and progression.
This lesson covers structure only. It does not provide real HKEAA papers or high-score student exemplars.

units.title: Drawing, Aesthetics and Design Thinking
units.intro: Aligned to F.4 Scheme “Creative Practice 2”: drawing skills, aesthetic/design thinking, material exploration and presentation skills. Builds observation, composition and material foundations for later theme work. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Observation and Drawing Basics: Line, Shape, Composition
cards: Drawing from observation starts with looking: overall shape and proportion first, details later—not deepest shadows first.
Basic visual elements: line, shape, colour, texture, space. Organising principles: contrast, rhythm, balance, emphasis.
Try compositions such as rule of thirds, diagonal guides and empty space. Different compositions change where viewers look first.
Wucius Wong brought design principles into ink landscape, showing how structure can organise a picture.
[No cleared image yet] Later: self-made line/shape drills, or an official museum page about Wucius Wong (text + link).

lessons.title: Aesthetics, Design Thinking and Material Exploration
cards: Aesthetic/design thinking: define a problem → generate options → prototype → test/reflect → improve.
Material exploration: try the same theme in pencil, charcoal, ink, collage, etc., and note which medium best serves your intention.
Presentation skills: state your theme, why you chose the medium, and how composition and symbols carry meaning.
Practice: pick one everyday object; make it twice in two media; write three sentences comparing which fits your theme better.

lessons.title: Weekly Visual Diary: How to Observe and Record
cards: A visual diary is a year-long habit: each week record what you see and feel, plus small experiments, in images and short notes.
You can include quick compositions, colour notes, tiny material trials, and one “today I noticed…” line.
The point is not perfect pages but steady observation and reflection—later theme work will use these materials.
Tip: keep one small book or digital folder; date + place + one reflection sentence.
[No cleared image yet] Later: a blank visual-diary layout template (self-made).

lessons.title: Community observation: finding a theme from the environment
cards: Classroom observation: use teacher-provided or already available photos, clips, objects, or sketches in class to record the environment and your learning. No outing or exhibition visit is required.
Making can relate to community: public space, neighbourhood routines, local signs—then reconnect to your theme.
Pak Sheung Chuen often uses everyday actions and ready-mades to make housing/space experiences visible.
Lee Kit often uses household cloth and everyday objects to speak about private feeling and space—community and personal life can be read together.

Practice: in class, use teacher-provided or already available photos, objects, or sketches. Note three symbols, objects, or sounds and how each could become a theme question. Contemporary works: [no cleared image] — text only.

units.title: Self-Portrait, Artist Research and Theme Development
units.intro: Aligned to F.4 “Theme and Artist research and Presentation I (Self-Portrait)” and discovery prompts Self / Relationship / Story. lessons.title: Self-Portrait and Identity: Self, Relationship, Story
cards: A self-portrait is more than likeness: it can speak about identity, bodily experience, roles and social gaze.
School prompts can open three doors: Self (a collection of curiosities), Relationship (family objects), Story (conflict or tension).
Frida Kahlo used self-portrait to speak personal experience and cultural identity—the learning goal is how symbols tell a self, not copying a style for marks.
Wilson Shieh paints contemporary figures in gongbi to explore Hong Kong identity; David Hockney often paints family and looking—useful for a “relationship” theme.
Copyrighted/contemporary works: [no cleared image] — classroom text + museum/reliable encyclopedia sources; public-domain historic self-portraits can be added later.

quiz.question: A self-portrait can explore:
options: Identity, relationships, personal story and social gaze
quiz.answer: Identity, relationships, personal story and social gaze
quiz.explain: Self-portrait is a common entry to theme and identity research.

lessons.title: How to Do Artist Research and a Theme Presentation
cards: Artist-research steps: choose relevant artists → record basics → study form and context → link to your theme → write a personal view with evidence.
Use reliable sources: museums, galleries, textbooks, teacher notes; separate facts from opinions.
Presentation I suggested structure: theme question → self/relationship entry → 1–2 artist comparisons → next media experiments.
The research workbook should show process: drafts, experiments, failures and improvements—not only final pretty photos.
Reminder: no full real exam papers and no “high-score” student exemplars.

quiz.explain: Media experiments turn research into making.

quiz.explain: Progression and reflection matter in SBA.

units.title: Art History Intro: Ancient West and Chinese Art
units.intro: Aligned to F.4 Orientation / early weeks: ancient cave art, Egypt, Greek and Roman art, plus a Chinese art introduction. Build a compact timeline and keyword sense for form, function and cultural context; briefly introduce calligraphy/painting as visual language (pictographs / oracle bone / silk painting)—not a full-year ink course. No real exam papers. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Ancient West: Cave, Egypt, Greek, Roman
cards: Start art history by asking what images solved for people: record, belief, power, beauty or commemoration.
Prehistoric cave images often show animals and handprints; notice space, repetition and ritual feel—not photo-likeness.
Egyptian art often stresses order, proportional rules and afterlife / sacred hierarchy; profile figures and scale hierarchy are common visual codes.
Greek art often seeks balanced, idealised human proportion; Roman art often emphasises realistic portraiture, public architecture and imperial narrative.

Task: for each of the four periods, write one keyword + one sentence on function; later turn this into a group Art Dictionary / personal Timeline. [No cleared image yet] Museum open images may be added later with sources.

quiz.question: A good starting question for ancient art is?
options: What function and context did the work serve?
quiz.answer: What function and context did the work serve?
quiz.explain: Form should connect to function, belief and social context.

quiz.question: Egyptian art often uses proportion and pose to show ____ and sacred order.
quiz.explain: Hierarchical scale and fixed poses are common visual rules.

quiz.question: Match period to a common focus
quiz.explain: Each period has different functions and aesthetic priorities.

quiz.question: An Art Dictionary / Timeline mainly trains you to?
options: Organise keywords, period traits and simple presentation
quiz.answer: Organise keywords, period traits and simple presentation
quiz.explain: Dictionary and timeline are starter organising tools.

lessons.title: Chinese Art Intro and Calligraphy–Painting Visual Language
cards: A gentle Chinese art entry point: writing and image telling stories together—pictographs, oracle-bone script and bronze motifs are visual communication.
Early images such as Warring States silk paintings often link ritual, afterlife and identity—look at line, symbol and spatial layout.
Calligraphy and painting often share language: brush energy, empty space and rhythm structure a surface, not only ‘correct characters’.
Intro goal: recognise a few visual codes (line, symbol, void) and describe one work’s form plus a possible context in short sentences.
Task: choose one pictograph or vessel motif, copy/draw it once, and write two lines: lines you see + possible meaning. [No cleared image yet] Add museum open images later with credit.

quiz.question: In VA class, pictographs / oracle-bone script are best treated as?
quiz.explain: Writing and image form a shared visual-language tradition.

quiz.question: Beyond character shape, calligraphy–painting intro also watches brush energy, rhythm and ____.
quiz.explain: Empty space (void) is part of pictorial structure.

quiz.question: When describing an early Chinese image, include?

quiz.question: Match intro focus

answer.Brush energy: Line and rhythm organise the surface

quiz.explain: Three doors into reading visual language.

units.title: Theme Seeds: Self, Relationship, Story
units.intro: Aligned to F.4 Discovery / Creative Assignments prompts: Self (curiosity collection), Relationship (family object), Story (conflict or tension). Before self-portrait research (U4), practise turning everyday objects and experiences into developable theme questions; link to the visual diary (U3). No high-score exemplars; no real exam papers. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Three Doors: Collection, Family Object, Conflict
cards: Theme seeds work best when they are small and real—start from something you care about, not a vague mega-topic.
Self: gather a small ‘curiosity collection’ (tickets, stones, packaging, old things). Ask: why keep this? which side of me does it show?
Relationship: choose one family object; note who uses it, when, and any rules or memories—objects can narrate relationships.
Story: use a ‘little person’ viewpoint to spot conflict or tension in an environment (crowding, waiting, rules, misunderstanding); sketch scene and feeling.
[No cleared image yet] Later: a three-door worksheet template (self-made).

lessons.title: From Seed to Theme Question
cards: Rewrite the seed as a theme question—e.g. ‘How does this family object define care?’ ‘What tension sits in bodies and space while waiting?’
A strong question opens research and making: observe, interview, test media—not a one-word answer.
Next links: keep recording in the visual diary (U3), artist comparison and self-portrait trials (U4), material tests (U2).
Mini presentation shape: my seed → theme question → materials already gathered → media I will try next.
Reminder: demos teach structure and method only—no real HKEAA papers and no high-score student works.
